title: NoSQL & Caching
html:
NoSQL & Caching

Why non-relational at all

Not "faster" - different trade-offs. Relational databases give you joins, constraints and transactions across tables. Give some of that up and you can buy horizontal scale, flexible shape, or a data model that matches the question better.

Kind Shape Fits
Document nested records, queried by key or field one aggregate read together
Key-value opaque value by key caches, sessions, counters
Wide-column rows with many sparse columns very high write volume, time series
Graph nodes and edges as first-class relationship traversal
Search inverted index text relevance, faceting

The honest default is still relational. Choose otherwise when you can name the property you need that it does not give you.

Modelling documents

Model around the queries, not around normal forms. If a screen always shows an order with its lines, store them together and read once.

The costs of that choice, which you accept deliberately:

  • Duplication. Denormalised copies must be updated in more than one place.
  • Unbounded arrays. An array that grows without limit eventually exceeds the document size limit and makes every read expensive. Cap it, or move it to its own collection.
  • No cross-document transaction, or only a limited one. Design so that a single logical change touches a single document where you can.

Caching

Caching trades freshness for speed, and the whole difficulty is the freshness half.

Strategies. Cache-aside (read, miss, load, store) is the common one and puts you in control. Read-through and write-through hide it behind the data layer. Write-behind is fastest and risks losing writes.

Invalidation is the hard part. Options: a TTL, which bounds staleness without needing to know what changed; explicit eviction on write, which is exact but easy to miss a path; or versioned keys, where the key itself contains a version so old entries are simply never read again.

Whichever you choose, decide the staleness window explicitly and write it down. "Cached" without a stated window is a bug waiting to be reported as a mystery.

Every key gets a TTL unless there is a stated reason it must live forever. It is the difference between a cache and a memory leak with a lookup API.

Key naming. Prefix by application and entity - app:entity:id:version. Unscoped keys collide the first time something else shares the instance.

Failure modes worth knowing

  • Stampede. A popular key expires and every request rebuilds it at once. Fix with a short lock, or by refreshing slightly before expiry.
  • Penetration. Repeated requests for something that does not exist, each missing the cache and hitting the database. Cache the negative result briefly.
  • Avalanche. Many keys expiring together. Jitter the TTLs.
  • Unbounded scans. Enumerating all keys on a live instance blocks it. Use an incremental cursor.

Consistency

CAP says that under a network partition you choose availability or consistency. Note the condition: it says nothing about normal operation, and most systems are not partitioned most of the time.

More useful day to day is what your store promises when it is healthy: read-your-writes, monotonic reads, eventual convergence. Know which you have, because "eventually consistent" plus a read immediately after a write is a bug report.

Common mistakes

  • Choosing a document store to avoid schema design, then discovering the schema lives in the application anyway.
  • Caching without a TTL or an invalidation story.
  • Caching a value derived from data that changes more often than the TTL.
  • Treating the cache as a source of truth and losing data when it restarts.
